The Dime Savings Bank of Brooklyn building at 9 Dekalb Avenue at Fleet Street in the Civic Center area of Brooklyn, New York City was built in 1906-08 and was designed by Mowbray & Uffinger in the Classical Revival style.. It was significantly enlarged by Halsey, McCormack & Helmer in 1931-32. The interior of the building is "remarkable" (AIA Guide) and features large gilded Mercury-head dimes and twelve red marble columns supporting the rotunda; these were added in the 1931-32 expansion. (Sources: Guide to NYC Landmarks (4th ed.) and AIA Guide to NYC (5th ed.)) The Dime Savings Bank of Brooklyn was later renamed to be the Dime Savings Bank of New York.

Samarium's new electron completes the electron pole, which consists of four electrons in the framework and a central electron. Two electrons are missing to complete the pole. According to the 4th rule, samarium can borrow these missing electrons from other samarium atoms, forming dimers and trimers. Agglomerates of two and three atoms partially block valence electrons. Therefore, samarium has a valence of +2. Individual samarium atoms have a valence of +3. Europium, according to the 4th rule, reproduces the electron capture effect. The atom lacks one electron to complete the pole, and it can borrow it from a neighboring atom. The mutual filling of electrons between two europium atoms results in a valence of +2. An individual europium atom has a valence of +3. Gadolinium has a fully formed pole cap of 7 electrons, and the electrons of this pole are inert, according to the 5th rule. Gadolinium has a valence of +3 and cannot form dimers. The new electron in the terbium atom, according to the first rule, is located on the opposite side of the pole and becomes a valence electron. Terbium, according to the sixth rule, has valences of +3 and +4. The new electron in dysprosium, according to the second rule, forms the opposite electron pole. Since the new pole consists of two electrons, dysprosium has a valence of +3 and rarely +4 due to partial blocking of the pole by electrons. The new electron in holmium completely blocks the ability of the pole electrons to form chemical bonds. Holmium has a valence of +3. Erbium, like gadolinium, has a valence of only +3 for the same reason as holmium. The new electron in thulium forms part of a daisy-like (frame) structure of four electrons. According to the second rule, a thulium atom can form dimers and trimers by blocking one valence electron from each thulium atom. In such an agglomeration, thulium atoms have a valence of +2. If the atoms are separated, their valence is +3. The new electron of the ytterbium atom forms a daisy-like structure with five electrons (petals). The atom lacks one electron to complete the structure. Therefore, ytterbium exhibits partial oxidizing properties, reducing its metallic chemical properties as a valence electron donor. An ytterbium atom can capture electrons from a neighboring atom, forming dimers (mutual filling of the electron shell). Ytterbium is unique among the lanthanides in its chemical properties.

Lutetium's new electron completely fills the pole, making it inert. Therefore, lutetium's valence is exclusively +3.

Filling the poles with 7 electrons on each side (the daisy chain) ensures repeatability of the chemical properties of 14 elements from cerium to lutetium and divides the lanthanide group into two subgroups with identical chemical properties.
